newsitem.title: THAILAND: Falling Thai stocks battered by baht rumours. [CORRECTED 12:20 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Falling Thai stocks battered by baht rumours. [CORRECTED 12:20 GMT]

text.p: Thai stocks, battered to 53-month lows by an unabated stream of bad news, are being pummeled this week by renewed market rumours of a baht devaluation, analysts said on Tuesday.
(Corrects time reference to a 53-month low from a 3-1/2 year low)
Market analysts said the rumour, mostly originating in Singapore, was a major factor in the stock market's nearly 10 percent fall over the last four sessions.

Repeated denials by Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan and the Bank of Thailand that a baht devaluation was planned failed to dispel the rumours or shore up the currency, which fell to 26.00 to the dollar last week from about 25.50 in December.

"I have seen a tendency for the market to look at things negatively. I don't see any immediate change or any single factor that could push up the market," said Mike Stead, head of research at Union Securities Plc.

Stead said sentiment on the baht would dictate the bourse's immediate performance. "The market has potential to go back up to 800 on the assumption that it was not hit by further panic on the baht," he said.

The composite SET Index hovered around 765 points late on Tuesday, up slightly on a technical rebound, brokers said. The index was at 1,000.73 in mid-November and 1,415.04 a year ago. It is at its lowest level since September 1, 1992 when it dropped to 753.53.

Chatchai Kittikun, technical analyst at Asia Equity Thailand, agreed with Stead and other analysts that the government was not expected to devalue the baht soon but he said it should take effective moves to stop currency speculation.

"I don't think it's enough to just say there will not be a devaluation. More baht rumours and speculation will persist so long as the central bank does not set a clear target how far it will let the baht fall," Chatchai said.

Brokers said foreign fund managers began picking up discounted Thai stocks in early January but the baht's recent depreciation against the dollar had prompted them to try to minimise foreign exchange losses by selling baht-denominated stocks in their portfolios.

The weakening baht has forced the government to keep interest rates high in the past month partly to discourage flight of local funds to the dollar. High short-term interest rates hurt the stock market.
Thai stocks have struggled through tough times since mid-1996, when sharply slowing exports and a high current-account deficit clouded the Thai economic picture.
Stead said although the current-account deficit -- estimated at 8.2 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 -- showed signs of easing, investors had not seen any export improvement.
Most analysts saw solid support for the market at 700-720. Chatchai of Asia Equity said he has advised investors to start accumulating major bank stocks.
"I think we could safely buy major banks now. I don't see Bangkok Bank going below 165 baht and Thai Farmers Bank 104-105 baht at the worst scenario," he said.
Bangkok Bank and Thai Farmers Bank traded at 177 baht and 117 baht, respectively, late on Tuesday against recent highs of 228 and 174 baht on September 30.
Analysts said bank and finance company earnings had declined in line with the slowing economy and a prolonged slump of the Thai property sector.
